opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Today’s readings left me feeling like I was missing something. At first, they seemed straightforward: believe and be saved, do not believe and be condemned. But the more I sat with them, the more I felt there had to be something deeper connecting all of this.

Moses climbs the mountain carrying the tablets and stands before God. He proclaims God’s glory and then asks something unexpected: take us as your own. He asks God to remain with them even though they are a stiff-necked people. Moses is not standing before God defending the faithful. He is interceding for people who repeatedly resist, doubt, and turn away. The first reading immediately introduces tension: human resistance exists, yet God still pursues.

Then Corinthians gives instruction that feels important: mend your ways, encourage one another, agree with one another, live in peace. Paul writes as though change remains possible. Encouragement would make little sense if people were fixed permanently in place. Community itself assumes movement, growth, correction, and transformation.

Then comes the Gospel and perhaps the line that unsettles most people: whoever believes in Him will not be condemned, but whoever does not believe has already been condemned. At first, this feels like two groups permanently separated. Yet immediately before this, John reminds us that God did not send His Son into the world to condemn the world, but that the world might be saved through Him.

So what exactly is condemnation here?

Maybe condemnation is not simply punishment imposed from outside. In John’s Gospel, it often sounds more like separation from the light when the light is offered. The light enters the world, and humanity responds to it in different ways.

This led me to another question: how can people not believe? Churches exist everywhere. Bibles are everywhere. Movies, statues, graveyards, worship, and believers themselves — Christianity surrounds much of human culture. How can some still not believe?

Perhaps because awareness and encounter are not the same thing. The disciples physically walked beside Christ and still doubted. Scripture repeatedly shows that exposure alone does not create faith. Christianity seems to claim something deeper than awareness — relationship, encounter, participation.

And perhaps this is where all three readings connect. Moses says: Remain with these difficult people anyway. Paul says: Encourage one another toward peace. John says: " The light has entered the world. All three assume movement is still possible.

Maybe the deeper question is not whether believers and non-believers exist together — clearly they do. Maybe the deeper question is what kind of God continues entering places where belief and unbelief live side by side.

The answer these readings seem to give is this: a God who stays with stiff-necked people. A God who keeps sending messengers. A God who enters resistance rather than avoiding it. A God who continues inviting.

And maybe this is the part I was missing.

The readings do not merely describe two categories of people. They are revealing the character of God.
